Convert the dissociation energy into a frequency, then see which part of the spectrum it
falls in.
**Step 1 — convert the energy to joules.**
E = 11 eV
= 11 x 1·6 x 10⁻¹⁹
= **1·76 x 10⁻¹⁸ J**
**Step 2 — find the frequency from E = hν.**
ν = E/h
= 1·76 x 10⁻¹⁸/6·626 x 10⁻³⁴
= **2·66 x 10¹⁵ Hz**
**Step 3 — find the wavelength, which is easier to place.**
λ = c/ν
= 3 x 10⁸/2·66 x 10¹⁵
= 1·13 x 10⁻⁷ m
= **113 nm**
**Step 4 — identify the region.** Visible light runs from about **400 nm to 700 nm** ✓
At 113 nm the radiation is well **below** the violet end, so it lies in the
**ultraviolet** ✓
**The spectrum, by wavelength.**
microwave: **1 mm to 30 cm**
infrared: **700 nm to 1 mm**
visible: **400 to 700 nm**
ultraviolet: **10 to 400 nm** ✓ - where 113 nm falls
X-rays: below 10 nm
**A faster route, in electron volts.** Visible photons carry between about **1·8 eV**
(red) and **3·1 eV** (violet) ✓ An 11 eV photon is three to six times more energetic than
any visible photon, so it must be ultraviolet or beyond - and 11 eV is too small for
X-rays, which start around 100 eV.
**The useful shortcut.**
λ(nm) = **1240/E(eV)**
so 1240/11 = **113 nm** ✓ in one step, and worth memorising.
**Why the question says "minimum frequency".** Any photon of **at least** this energy can
break the bond; lower-energy photons cannot, however many arrive ✓ This threshold
behaviour is the same quantum principle that governs the photoelectric effect.
**Reading the distractors.** **Visible** ✗ needs 1·8 to 3·1 eV, **infrared** ✗ less than
1·8 eV, and **microwave** ✗ less than 0·001 eV - all far below 11 eV ✓
∴ ultraviolet region.

Reflection reverses the **direction of travel** and, at a perfect conductor, also
**flips the sign** of the electric field.
**Step 1 — change the direction of propagation.** The incident wave
E = E₀ î cos(kz − ωt)
travels along **+z**, since the phase (kz − ωt) is constant for z increasing with t ✓
After reflection the wave travels along **−z**, which requires the phase
**(kz + ωt)** ✓
**Step 2 — apply the boundary condition at the wall.** At the surface of a **perfect
conductor** the tangential electric field must vanish:
E_incident + E_reflected = 0 at z = a ✓
so the reflected field must be the **negative** of the incident one at the wall. This
gives the reflected wave an amplitude of **−E₀**.
**Step 3 — keep the polarisation.** The wall is "optically inactive", so it does not
rotate the plane of polarisation ✓ The reflected field stays along **î**.
**Step 4 — assemble.**
**E_r = −E₀ î cos(kz + ωt)** ✓
**Why the sign flip is physically necessary.** A perfect conductor has free charges that
rearrange instantly to cancel any field inside it ✓ The only way the total tangential
field can be zero at the surface is for the reflected wave to arrive exactly out of
phase - a **phase change of π** on reflection, which is what the minus sign records.
**The standing wave that results.** Adding the two waves:
E_total = E₀ î[cos(kz − ωt) − cos(kz + ωt)]
= 2E₀ î sin(kz) sin(ωt) ✓
a **standing wave** with a **node** wherever sin(kz) = 0 - and in particular at the wall,
exactly as the boundary condition demands.
**The optical parallel.** Light reflecting from a denser medium undergoes the same π
phase change ✓ It is why the centre of Newton's rings in reflected light is **dark**, and
why a thin film one quarter-wavelength thick works as an anti-reflection coating.
**Reading the distractors.** **−E₀ î cos(kz − ωt)** ✗ has the sign flip but keeps the
wave travelling in the **same** direction - it has not reflected at all. **E₀ î cos(kz +
ωt)** ✗ reverses the direction but omits the phase change, so the field at the wall would
be 2E₀ instead of zero. **E₀ î sin(kz − ωt)** ✗ changes neither direction nor sign,
merely the phase by π/2 ✓
∴ E_r = −E₀ î cos(kz + ωt).

Note: the printed key gives the second option, E₀ î cos(kz + ωt). That form travels in
the right direction but carries no phase reversal, so the tangential field at the
perfectly reflecting wall would be 2E₀ rather than the required zero. The key has been
corrected to the third option.

Read ω and k off the wave equation, then test each of the four statements.
**Step 1 — identify the parameters.** Comparing
E = 10 cos(10⁷t + kx) ĵ
with the general form E₀ cos(ωt + kx):
amplitude **E₀ = 10 V/m**
angular frequency **ω = 10⁷ rad s⁻¹**
**Step 2 — find the wave number.** In free space ω/k = c, so
k = ω/c
= 10⁷/(3 x 10⁸)
= **0·0333 rad m⁻¹**
**Step 3 — find the wavelength.**
λ = 2π/k
= 6·283/0·0333
= **188·5 m** ✓
**Step 4 — find the direction of travel.** The phase is **(ωt + kx)**, with a **plus**
sign, so a point of constant phase has x **decreasing** as t increases ✓ The wave travels
along **−x**.
**Step 5 — test the four statements.**
**(1) λ = 188·4 m** ✓ **correct**
**(2) k = 0·33 rad/m** ✗ the value is 0·033, ten times smaller
**(3) amplitude = 10 V/m** ✓ **correct**, read straight off
**(4) propagating along +x** ✗ the plus sign in the phase means **−x**
**Step 6 — pick the pair.** Statements **(1) and (3)** are the correct ones ✓
**The two traps in this question.** The factor of ten in k, and the sign in the phase ✓
Both are easy to misread at speed, and the options are built so that each error leads to
a different wrong pair.
**A consistency check.** If λ = 188·4 m then
k = 2π/λ = 6·283/188·4 = **0·0333 rad m⁻¹** ✓ confirming that statements (1) and (2)
cannot **both** be right - and that (1) is the one that survives.
**The rule for direction.**
**(kx − ωt)** → travelling along **+x**
**(kx + ωt)** → travelling along **−x** ✓
The sign between the two terms, not the order in which they are written, is what decides.
**The frequency, for completeness.** ν = ω/2π = 10⁷/6·283 = **1·59 MHz** - in the medium
wave radio band, which fits a wavelength of 188 m ✓
∴ (1) and (3).

Refractive index is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the
medium, and both speeds come from the same formula.
**Step 1 — write the speed of light in each.**
in vacuum: c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀)
in the medium: v = 1/√(μ ε) ✓
**Step 2 — form the refractive index.**
n = c/v
= √(μ ε)/√(μ₀ ε₀)
= **√(μ_r ε_r)**
where μ_r = μ/μ₀ is the relative permeability and ε_r the relative permittivity, or
**dielectric constant** ✓
**Step 3 — match to the question's symbols.** With μ₀ standing for the permeability and
k₀ for the dielectric constant of the medium:
**n = √(μ₀ k₀)** ✓
**Why it is a square root.** The speed of a wave depends on the **square root** of the
product of the medium's two electromagnetic constants, just as the speed on a string
goes as √(T/μ) ✓ The index therefore inherits that square root.
**A worked instance.** For water at optical frequencies, μ_r ≈ 1 and ε_r ≈ 1·77:
n = √(1 x 1·77) = **1·33** ✓ the familiar refractive index of water.
**Why μ_r is usually ignored.** For most transparent materials μ_r is within a fraction
of a per cent of 1, so **n ≈ √ε_r** ✓ That is Maxwell's relation, one of the strongest
early confirmations that light is an electromagnetic wave.
**A caution about frequency.** The ε_r measured at low frequency does not always give the
optical index - water has ε_r = 80 at low frequencies, which would predict n = 8·9 ✗ The
molecules cannot follow an optical field, so the effective ε_r drops to 1·77 ✓
**Reading the distractors.** **1/√(μ₀k₀)** ✗ is proportional to the **speed** in the
medium, not the index - it gets **smaller** in a denser medium, when n should grow.
**μ₀k₀** ✗ and **1/(μ₀k₀)** ✗ omit the square root ✓ For water they would give 1·77 and
0·56 instead of 1·33.
**A check on the dimensions.** With μ_r and ε_r both dimensionless, their product's
square root is dimensionless ✓ as a refractive index must be.
∴ √(μ₀k₀).

In an electromagnetic wave the ratio of the field amplitudes equals the **speed of
light**, and that speed is ω/k.
**Step 1 — state the amplitude relation.** For a plane wave in vacuum,
**E₀/B₀ = c** ✓
**Step 2 — write c in terms of the wave parameters.** For any wave,
c = νλ = (ω/2π)(2π/k) = **ω/k** ✓
**Step 3 — combine.**
E₀/B₀ = ω/k
and cross-multiplying,
**E₀k = B₀ω** ✓
**Where the relation comes from.** Substituting the two given waves into Faraday's law
in differential form, ∂E/∂x = −∂B/∂t:
E₀k cos(kx − ωt) = B₀ω cos(kx − ωt)
so **E₀k = B₀ω** at every point and instant ✓ The relation is not an extra assumption -
it is forced by Maxwell's equations.
**Checking the dimensions.**
[E₀k] = (V m⁻¹)(m⁻¹) = **V m⁻²**
[B₀ω] = (T)(s⁻¹) = **T s⁻¹**
and since 1 T = 1 V s m⁻², T s⁻¹ = **V m⁻²** ✓ the two sides match.
**A numerical illustration.** Sunlight at the Earth's surface has E₀ ≈ 1000 V m⁻¹, so
B₀ = E₀/c = 1000/(3 x 10⁸) = **3·3 x 10⁻⁶ T** ✓ a few per cent of the Earth's own
magnetic field - which is why the magnetic part of light is so hard to detect directly.
**Why the two fields are in phase.** Both are written as sin(kx − ωt) with no phase
offset ✓ E and B peak together, vanish together, and are mutually perpendicular as well
as perpendicular to the direction of travel.
**Reading the distractors.** **E₀B₀ = k** ✗ fails on dimensions - a product of fields is
not a wave number. **E₀ω = B₀k** ✗ has the relation **inverted**, giving E₀/B₀ = k/ω =
1/c, so the magnetic field would be 10⁸ times the electric - the commonest error here.
**None of these** ✗ is unnecessary ✓
∴ E₀k = B₀ω.
